title: Population oral health, inequalities & community prevention
blurb: How oral health is measured, why it is unequal, and the community and population measures (water fluoridation, supervised toothbrushing, sugar policy) that reach everyone.
question: Your practice is asked to help with a local project because children in one part of town have far more tooth decay than children a few miles away. Why might that be, how would the project measure the problem, and which community measures are most likely to make a difference?

teach.h: From one patient to whole communities
teach.body: Chairside advice helps one patient at a time and depends on that person acting on it. A population approach looks at the oral health of whole groups and changes the conditions they live in, so that the healthy choice becomes the easy choice. Measures that reach everyone automatically, like fluoride in water or less sugar in drinks, need no effort from individuals. That is why they tend to narrow the gap between the healthiest and least healthy groups.

steps.label: Policy (upstream)
steps.sub: Water fluoridation, Soft Drinks Industry Levy

steps.label: Community
steps.sub: Supervised toothbrushing and varnish in nurseries and schools

teach.caption: Upstream measures prevent disease in large numbers of people at once; downstream care deals with individuals, often after disease has started.

teach.body: Oral disease follows a social gradient: the more deprived an area, the more tooth decay and tooth loss its people tend to have. This is driven by the wider determinants of health, such as income, education, housing, employment, diet, access to services and culture. Tooth decay is one of the most common reasons young children are admitted to hospital in England. Sugar, tobacco, alcohol and poor hygiene also cause heart disease, cancers and diabetes, so tackling these common risk factors improves general health too.

letters.sub: Count per person; lower case 'dmft' for baby teeth

teach.caption: Averaged across a group, DMFT shows how much decay a population has experienced. National surveys use it to compare areas and track change over time.

teach.body: Water fluoridation adjusts the natural fluoride in public water supplies to around 1 part per million (1 mg/L), the level that gives good protection against decay. It reaches everyone on that supply regardless of income or behaviour, so it helps reduce inequalities. Parts of England, such as Birmingham and much of the West Midlands, have long-standing schemes. In England, the Health and Care Act 2022 gave the Secretary of State for Health the power to introduce new schemes, following public consultation.

Childsmile is Scotland's national programme: supervised toothbrushing in nurseries and schools, fluoride varnish for young children, and toothbrush and toothpaste packs for families. Designed to Smile is the Welsh equivalent, built around supervised toothbrushing in nurseries and schools and oral health support from birth. In England, supervised toothbrushing schemes in nurseries and schools are targeted at areas of greatest need. Other measures include oral health training for care home staff and the Soft Drinks Industry Levy, a tax on sugary drinks introduced in 2018.

teach.caption: Collaboration is essential: in England, local authorities have been responsible for oral health improvement since 2013, working with the NHS, schools, GPs, pharmacists and social care.

teach.text: Health education alone (leaflets, talks) can actually widen inequalities, because people with more resources are more likely to act on it. Upstream measures such as water fluoridation and sugar policy work without relying on individual effort.

items: Population approaches change conditions for whole groups; upstream measures reduce inequalities.
Oral disease follows a social gradient driven by the wider determinants of health.
DMFT/dmft measures caries experience; prevalence = existing cases, incidence = new cases.
Water fluoridation at about 1 ppm; Childsmile (Scotland) and Designed to Smile (Wales); supervised toothbrushing in England.
Plan community care: assess need, set aims, plan with partners, deliver, evaluate.

summary: You can now explain the difference between individual and population approaches, describe oral health inequalities and their causes, measure caries with DMFT and distinguish prevalence from incidence, describe water fluoridation and UK community programmes, use the Ottawa Charter to describe health promotion, and outline how community oral health care is planned and evaluated with partners.

A.q: What does the 'M' stand for in the DMFT index?
options: Teeth missing for any reason at all
A.why: In DMFT, M counts teeth missing because of decay, alongside decayed and filled teeth.

whyNot.1: Teeth lost for other reasons, such as orthodontics or trauma, aren't counted as caries experience.
whyNot.3: Mobility from gum disease isn't part of a caries index.

A.q: To what level is fluoride adjusted in UK water fluoridation schemes?
A.why: Fluoridation schemes adjust fluoride in drinking water to around 1 part per million (1 mg/L).

whyNot.0: 0.1 ppm is too low to give useful protection.

A.q: Why does water fluoridation help reduce oral health inequalities?
options: It replaces the need for toothbrushing
It needs no effort from individuals
A.why: It reaches everyone on the water supply automatically, regardless of income, knowledge or behaviour.

whyNot.0: It reaches everyone on the supply, whatever their income.
whyNot.1: It adds to, and doesn't replace, brushing with fluoride toothpaste.
whyNot.3: It benefits people of all ages.

B.q: Which national programme provides supervised toothbrushing and fluoride varnish for young children in Scotland?
B.why: Childsmile is Scotland's national child oral health improvement programme.

whyNot.0: Designed to Smile is the Welsh programme.
whyNot.1: Smokefree is an NHS stop-smoking campaign.
whyNot.2: Change4Life is a general healthy-lifestyle campaign in England.

B.q: A survey finds 25% of 5-year-olds in an area currently have decay experience. What does this figure describe?
B.why: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at a point in time.

whyNot.0: Incidence counts new cases over a period, not existing cases at one time.
whyNot.3: A yearly rate would describe new cases, which is incidence.

B.q: Which of these is an 'upstream' population measure?
B.why: A sugar levy changes the environment for the whole population, so it acts upstream.

whyNot.1: A filling treats disease in one person, downstream.
whyNot.2: Chairside advice is an individual, downstream measure.
whyNot.3: A scale and polish is individual treatment.

C.q: What pattern does oral disease usually follow across the UK population?
options: It is the same in every area
It is highest in the wealthiest areas
It is worse in more deprived areas
C.why: Oral disease follows a social gradient: more deprived areas tend to have more decay and tooth loss.

whyNot.0: There are large differences between areas.
whyNot.1: Wealthier areas generally have less disease.
whyNot.3: Oral disease affects all ages, including young children.

C.q: When planning a community oral health programme, what should come first?
options: Ordering the toothbrush and paste packs
C.why: Planning starts by assessing need, using survey data and local information, so the programme targets the right problems.

whyNot.0: Evaluation comes at the end, to see whether it worked.
whyNot.1: Delivery comes after aims are set and partners agreed.
whyNot.2: Ordering resources is part of delivery, after the needs are known.

C.q: Which Ottawa Charter action area does a tax on sugary drinks fit best?
C.why: A sugar levy is a government policy that makes the healthier choice easier for everyone.

whyNot.1: Personal skills means teaching individuals, such as toothbrushing sessions.
whyNot.2: Reorienting services means changing how health services work, such as a focus on prevention.
whyNot.3: Community action is local people working together, not national tax policy.

reteach.title: Fence at the top of the cliff
reteach.question: People keep falling off a cliff. You could park more ambulances at the bottom, or build a fence at the top. Which is population oral health?

blocks.body: Fillings, extractions and even chairside advice are the ambulances at the bottom: essential, but they deal with people one at a time, often after they've fallen. Water fluoridation, sugar taxes and supervised toothbrushing in nurseries are the fence at the top: they stop large numbers of people falling in the first place, especially those who would never get to the ambulance. A good system needs both, but the fence does more for fairness.

blocks.text: Childsmile = Scotland. Designed to Smile = Wales. Don't mix them up.

explain.body: Oral disease follows a social gradient. Income, education, housing, diet, access to services and culture all shape oral health. Common risk factors (sugar, tobacco, alcohol) link oral and general disease.

explain.caption: Illustrative social gradient: decay tends to rise step by step with deprivation.

test.q: Which is an example of a wider determinant of oral health?
test.why: Income is a social determinant that influences diet, access to care and many health behaviours.

whyNot.0: Enamel thickness is a biological feature of the tooth.
whyNot.2: Tooth shape is anatomical, not a wider determinant.
whyNot.3: Root number is anatomy, not a social factor.

explain.body: DMFT counts decayed, missing (due to decay) and filled permanent teeth; dmft for baby teeth. Prevalence is existing cases at one time; incidence is new cases over a period.

test.q: A child has 2 decayed, 1 extracted because of decay and 3 filled baby teeth. What is their dmft?
test.why: dmft adds decayed (2), missing due to decay (1) and filled (3) to give 6.

whyNot.1: 5 leaves out the decayed or missing teeth.

explain.body: Water fluoridation (about 1 ppm), supervised toothbrushing and varnish programmes (Childsmile, Designed to Smile, targeted schemes in England), and the Soft Drinks Industry Levy.

options: An English tax on sugary soft drinks
A Welsh child oral health programme
test.why: Designed to Smile is the Welsh Government's national child oral health improvement programme.

whyNot.0: Scotland's child programme is Childsmile, and it isn't a fluoridation scheme.
whyNot.1: The sugar tax is the Soft Drinks Industry Levy.

explain.body: Assess need, set SMART aims, plan with partners, deliver, evaluate. Partners include local authorities, schools, health visitors, GPs, pharmacists and care homes.

test.q: In England, which body has been responsible for local oral health improvement since 2013?
test.why: Local authorities took on responsibility for oral health improvement in 2013, working with NHS and other partners.

whyNot.0: The GDC regulates dental professionals; it doesn't run oral health improvement.
whyNot.2: The BDA is a professional association and trade union.
whyNot.3: Practices help, but they don't hold the local responsibility.
